(i) rheological variables were associated positively with cardiovascular risk factors, (ii) rheological variables and interleukin 6 were associated independently with cardiovascular disease, and (iii) hormone replacement therapy reduced the differences between pre‐ and post‐menopausal blood rheology.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of blood rheology in cardiovascular disease.
the associations of rheological variables with major cardiovascular risk factors and with the prevalence of CVD.
the role of blood rheology in aetiology of CVD.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

rheological variables are associated with some cardiovascular risk factors, and with prevalent cardiovascular disease; but that the strength of the associations is modest and that they are unlikely to be of major importance in cardiovascular epidemiology.
blood viscosity is not associated with cardiovascular risk, and that plasma interleukin‐ 6 is not associated with risk factors or prevalent disease.
rheological variables are associated with major cardiovascular risk factors, but that the associations with CVD are relatively weak and not consistent.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

rheological variables are associated with cardiovascular risk factors, but only plasma viscosity and relative blood viscosity are independently associated with prevalent C.V.D. after risk factor adjustment.
blood viscosity and fibrinogenicity are associated with cardiovascular risk factors, but not with cardiovascular disease.

rheological variables are associated with cardiovascular risk factors, but only a few of them are associated with cardiovascular disease, and that plasma viscosity and red blood cell aggregation may be the most useful of the rheological variables for cardiovascular risk prediction.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the associations of blood viscosity with risk factors and cardiovascular disease are weak and inconsistent, whereas plasma viscosity shows stronger and more consistent associations.
the associations of blood rheology with cardiovascular disease are weak, and are largely explained by the associations of the rheology variables with other risk factors.
the associations of blood rheology with cardiovascular risk factors are similar to those of CVD itself, and that the rheological variables are not independent predictors of cardiovascular disease.
